decks.title: The Making of a Global World — Part 1: Silk Routes, Food, Conquest and Disease
goals: Describe how silk routes and the movement of foods linked distant parts of the world
Explain how European conquest of the Americas, germs and trade reshaped the world economy
Explain why the centre of world trade moved westwards
Answer a source-based question and a 5-mark question the way examiners mark them

slides.heading: The Making of a Global World
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how goods, people, ideas and germs tied distant lands together, from ancient coastal trade to the conquest of the Americas. *(Board syllabus: these two topics only.)*

nodes.label: About 3000 BCE: Indus–West Asia coastal trade
Before the Christian Era to about 1400s: silk routes
1492: Columbus reaches the Americas
Mid-1500s: conquest of the Americas well under way
1700s: China and India still among the richest
Mid-1840s: potato famine in Ireland

visual.alt: Timeline of Part 1: Indus to West Asia coastal trade around 3000 BCE, the silk routes from before the Christian Era to about the fifteenth century, Columbus in 1492, the conquest of the Americas by the mid sixteenth century, China and India still among the richest in the eighteenth century, and the Irish potato famine in the mid 1840s
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Namaste! Look at the clothes you are wearing, the phone in your pocket, the chilli in your lunch. Each has travelled a long way to reach you. We call this globalisation, and we often think it is new. In this chapter we will find that the world has been weaving itself together for five thousand years. For your board exam, focus on two topics: the pre-modern world, and conquest, disease and trade.

slides.heading: Who travelled, and why?
slides.body_md: A **global world** grows when people, goods, money, ideas and even germs move between distant regions.

visual.alt: Table: traders travelled for profit, workers for a living, priests and pilgrims for faith, and refugees for safety; they carried goods, skills, ideas and values, and without knowing it, germs and diseases

slides.narration: Who made the world global? Not only kings and armies. Traders went looking for profit, workers for jobs, priests and pilgrims for faith, and some people simply ran from persecution at home. Each carried something: goods and money, but also skills, stories, beliefs and recipes. And every traveller carried something invisible too: germs. Keep this list in mind, because examiners often ask what moved along these early routes.

slides.heading: Ancient links across the seas

rows: Coastal trade between the Indus valley and West Asia, about 3000 BCE
Sea trade is at least five thousand years old
Cowrie shells from the Maldives found in China and East Africa
Cowries worked as money over huge distances
Germs spreading along trade routes, traced to at least the seventh century
Disease travelled with trade; by the thirteenth century the link is clear

visual.alt: Table of early evidence: Indus to West Asia trade around 3000 BCE shows ancient sea trade; Maldivian cowries in China and East Africa show shells used as money far away; germs spreading along trade routes from at least the seventh century show disease travelling with trade

slides.narration: Here are three clues historians use. First, around three thousand BCE, ships traded along the coast between the Indus valley and West Asia. Second, cowries, the little shells from the Maldives, turn up as far away as China and East Africa, because people used them as money. Third, germs: by the seventh century, and very clearly by the thirteenth, diseases were travelling along the same routes as traders.

slides.heading: The silk routes: what moved, and which way
slides.body_md: Not one road but **many routes over land and sea**, linking Asia with Europe and northern Africa, from before the Christian Era almost until the **fifteenth century**.

rows: Textiles and spices from India and Southeast Asia

visual.alt: Table of silk-route flows: silk, pottery, textiles and spices moved west; gold and silver moved east; religions, ideas, travellers and skills moved both ways

slides.narration: The name silk routes comes from one famous cargo: Chinese silk carried west. But silk was only part of the story. Fine Chinese pottery, Indian textiles and spices from India and Southeast Asia went the same way. In return, Europe paid in gold and silver, which flowed east into Asia. Notice the plural, routes. There were many, over mountains, deserts and seas, and they lasted more than a thousand years.

slides.heading: Trade and faith travelled together

nodes.label: Merchants meet at caravan towns and ports
Buddhism spreads from eastern India in several directions
Early Christian missionaries travel to Asia
A few centuries later, Muslim preachers follow
Trade routes become routes of culture

visual.alt: Flow: merchants meeting at caravan towns and ports opened the way for Buddhism spreading from eastern India, for early Christian missionaries, and later for Muslim preachers, so trade routes became routes of culture

slides.narration: Wherever merchants stop, people talk. Caravan towns and ports on the silk routes became meeting places for ideas as well as goods. Buddhism travelled out of eastern India along these routes to Central Asia and China. Christian preachers made the journey east in the early centuries, and Muslim teachers followed later. So when you write about the silk routes, never stop at goods. Culture travelled in the same caravans.

slides.heading: Quick check: the silk routes
slides.body_md: Choose the correct option.
slides.narration: Think about when the silk routes began and roughly when they faded.

slides.heading: Food on the move
slides.body_md: Food is one of the best ways to see **cultural exchange** across long distances.

rows: Noodles may have travelled west from China and become spaghetti in Italy
Or Arab traders may have taken pasta to Sicily around the fifth century
Similar foods appear in India and Japan
Old contacts that are hard to date

visual.alt: Table: noodles may have gone from China to Italy as spaghetti, or Arab traders may have taken pasta to Sicily; similar foods in India and Japan suggest old contacts; foods change as they travel

slides.narration: Think of a plate of spaghetti. One popular story says noodles travelled west from China and became Italian pasta. Another says Arab traders took pasta to Sicily, an island now part of Italy. Historians are not sure which is right, and that is fine. The lesson is that food moves with people and changes to suit local tastes. In your answers, say "it is believed", because the exact origin is uncertain.

slides.heading: Gifts from the Americas
slides.body_md: Many foods we call everyday reached **Asia and Europe** only about **five hundred years ago**.

headers: Food first grown in the Americas
rows: Europe (a staple of the poor), India
Europe; chillies reached India with Portuguese traders

visual.alt: Table of foods first grown in the Americas, potato, maize, tomato, chilli, groundnut, soya and sweet potato, and where they spread after 1492, including chillies reaching India with Portuguese traders

slides.narration: Here is a surprise for your next meal. Potatoes, tomatoes, chillies, maize and groundnuts were all first grown by the peoples of the Americas. They reached Europe and Asia only after Columbus crossed the Atlantic in fourteen ninety-two. Chillies are believed to have come to India with Portuguese traders. So a samosa or a plate of pav bhaji is a little lesson in world history.

slides.heading: The potato: a blessing and a trap

nodes.label: Potato reaches Europe from the Americas
Cheap, filling food for the poor
The poor are better fed and live longer
Ireland's poorest grow almost nothing else
Blight in the mid-1840s
Hundreds of thousands starve; many emigrate

visual.alt: Flow: the potato reached Europe, gave the poor cheap food so that many ate better and lived longer; Ireland's poorest came to grow almost nothing else; blight in the mid 1840s caused hundreds of thousands to starve and many to emigrate

slides.narration: The potato changed Europe. It was cheap and filling, and many poor families were better fed and lived longer. In Ireland, the poorest peasants came to depend on it almost completely. Then, in the mid eighteen forties, a disease called blight rotted the crop. With nothing else to eat, hundreds of thousands starved and many more emigrated. One crop brought both survival and disaster. That is a perfect evaluation point.

slides.heading: Quick check: new foods
slides.body_md: True or false?
slides.narration: Ask yourself where each crop was first grown, and when it could have reached Europe and Asia.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a source-based question, step by step
slides.body_md: Source (written by SOYL): *An imagined letter from a Venetian merchant in Alexandria, 1420, lists bales of Indian pepper and Chinese silk bought with silver from German mines, and mentions a scholar on the same ship carrying books on astronomy.*
bullets: Step 1 — Read the questions first.
Step 2 — (a) "Name one Asian good in the letter" (1 mark): pepper or silk, straight from the source.
Step 3 — (b) "How were the goods paid for?" (1 mark): silver, from the source.
Step 4 — (c) "What does the scholar show about trade routes?" (2 marks): source point (books travelled with goods) + knowledge point (religions like Buddhism also spread along trade routes).
Step 5 — Keep (c) to about 40 words.

rows: An Asian good named in the source
1 for the source point + 1 for wider knowledge

visual.alt: Table: part a earns one mark for an Asian good from the source, part b one mark for silver, part c two marks, one from the source and one from wider knowledge

slides.narration: Here is the method that works for every source. Read the questions first, so you read with a purpose. One-mark parts usually sit right in the source: pepper or silk, paid for with silver. The two-mark part asks you to think beyond the page. The scholar shows that ideas travelled with goods; you add, from your own knowledge, that faiths like Buddhism spread the same way. One point each, two marks.

slides.heading: The sixteenth century: oceans open up
slides.body_md: European sailors found a **sea route to Asia** and crossed the **Atlantic** to the Americas.

rows: A central meeting point of Indian Ocean trade
Still important, but Europeans enter the trade
Many directions, shared by many traders
Some flows expanded, others redirected towards Europe
Cut off from Asia, Europe and Africa
Linked to the rest of the world

visual.alt: Table: before the sixteenth century the Indian subcontinent was central to Indian Ocean trade with flows in many directions and the Americas cut off; from the sixteenth century Europeans entered the trade, redirected some flows towards Europe and linked the Americas to the world

slides.narration: In the fifteen hundreds the map of trade changed. Before then, the Indian subcontinent sat at the centre of a busy Indian Ocean world, where Indian, Arab, African and Southeast Asian traders shared the seas. Now European ships arrived, first by sailing round Africa, and others crossed the Atlantic to the Americas. Europeans expanded some old trade flows and steered others towards their own ports.

slides.heading: Silver and the legend of El Dorado

nodes.label: Stories of a golden city in South America
Expeditions set out to find El Dorado
Real wealth: silver mines in present-day Peru and Mexico
Silver ships to Europe
Europe richer; pays for Asian goods

visual.alt: Flow: stories of a golden city drew expeditions in search of El Dorado; the real wealth was silver mined in present-day Peru and Mexico, shipped to Europe, which became richer and paid for Asian goods

slides.narration: Europeans dreamed of gold. A legend spoke of El Dorado, a city of gold somewhere in South America, and expedition after expedition went looking for it. No such city was ever found. The real treasure was silver, dug from mines in places such as present-day Peru and Mexico. That silver made Europe richer and paid for spices, silk and cloth from Asia.

slides.heading: Conquest by germs

nodes.label: Americas isolated from other continents for thousands of years
No immunity to diseases common in Europe
Smallpox arrives with Europeans
Disease spreads ahead of the conquerors
Whole communities devastated; resistance collapses

visual.alt: Flow: long isolation meant no immunity; smallpox arriving with Europeans spread ahead of the conquerors and devastated whole communities so that resistance collapsed

slides.narration: The Spanish and Portuguese had guns and horses, but their deadliest weapon was invisible. The peoples of the Americas had been cut off from other continents for thousands of years, so their bodies had never met diseases like smallpox. Once it arrived, smallpox raced from village to village, often ahead of the Europeans themselves, killing huge numbers. Guns could be captured and used back. Germs could not.

slides.heading: Quick check: why smallpox?
slides.body_md: Decide whether the assertion and the reason are true, and whether the reason explains the assertion.
slides.narration: Is each statement true? Then ask whether the second really explains the first.

slides.heading: Who went to the Americas, and who was taken
columns:
**Europeans who chose to go**

- Escaping poverty and hunger
- Leaving crowded cities and deadly diseases
- Religious dissenters fleeing persecution
- Hoping for land and riches

**Africans who were forced to go**

- Captured and enslaved in Africa
- Made to work on plantations
- Growing cotton and sugar for European markets

visual.alt: Table: European settlers went mostly by choice to farm, trade and mine; enslaved Africans were forced to work on cotton and sugar plantations

slides.narration: Until the nineteenth century, life in Europe was hard for many. Poverty and hunger were common, cities were crowded and full of disease, and people with different religious beliefs were often persecuted. So thousands sailed to America. But not everyone crossing the ocean chose to. Millions of Africans were captured and enslaved, and forced to grow cotton and sugar on plantations for European buyers.

slides.heading: The centre of world trade moves west

nodes.label: China and India among the richest until well into the 1700s
From the 1400s China, by most accounts, turns away from overseas contact
Americas grow in importance: silver, crops, markets
Centre of world trade shifts westwards
Europe emerges as the centre

visual.alt: Flow: China and India were among the richest until well into the eighteenth century; China turned away from overseas contact from the fifteenth century and the Americas grew in importance, so the centre of world trade shifted westwards and Europe emerged as its centre

slides.narration: Here is a fact that surprises many students. Right up to the seventeen hundreds, China and India ranked with the wealthiest lands on earth, and they led Asian trade. So why did Europe end up at the centre? From the fifteenth century, China is said to have pulled back from overseas contacts. At the same time the Americas became a source of silver, crops and markets. Slowly, the centre of trade moved west.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a 5-mark answer that scores full marks
slides.body_md: Question: *Explain how the conquest of the Americas in the sixteenth century changed the world economy.* (about 120 words)
bullets: Step 1 — Open with one line: contact with the Americas created new flows of metals, crops and people.
Step 2 — Plan five distinct points: germs, silver, plantations and slavery, migration, the westward shift of trade.
Step 3 — Put a key term in each: smallpox, El Dorado or silver, enslaved Africans, religious dissenters, Europe as centre.
Step 4 — Do not write two points about silver.
Step 5 — Stop at about 120 words.

rows: Centre of trade shifts to Europe

visual.alt: Table of five planned points with key terms, one mark each: smallpox and immunity; silver and trade with Asia; plantations and enslaved Africans; European migration; the shift of the centre of trade to Europe

slides.narration: A five-mark answer needs five different ideas. Plan before you write. For the conquest of the Americas, the five boxes are germs, silver, plantations, migration and the shift of trade. Each point should carry a key word the examiner is looking for, such as smallpox or enslaved Africans. The usual mistake is to spend three points on silver and gold. Spread your answer across the five boxes.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: reading a world map
slides.body_md: Task (practice): *On an outline map of the world, locate and label (A) the country where silk came from, (B) the islands whose cowries were used as money, and (C) the European island hit by famine in the 1840s.*
bullets: Step 1 — Decode: silk → China; cowries → Maldives; famine → Ireland.
Step 2 — China: the large country of East Asia, north-east of India.
Step 3 — Maldives: a chain of tiny islands south-west of India and Sri Lanka.
Step 4 — Ireland: the island west of Great Britain.
Step 5 — Dot or shade, then write the full name.

visual.alt: Table of map clues: silk is China in East Asia; cowries are the Maldives south-west of India; the potato famine is Ireland, west of Great Britain

slides.narration: This chapter has no board map items, but a world map helps you picture the story. Turn each clue into a place. Silk means China. Cowries mean the Maldives, those tiny islands south-west of India. The famine means Ireland, the island to the west of Great Britain. Find a landmark first, then mark and label neatly. The same method will serve you in every map question.

slides.heading: Quick check: putting events in order
slides.body_md: Arrange these developments from earliest to latest.
slides.narration: Write a date or century beside each event first, then order them.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Trade, work, faith, learning, escape from persecution
Indus–West Asia trade about 3000 BCE; Maldivian cowries in China and East Africa
Many land and sea routes; silk, pottery, spices west; gold and silver east; Buddhism and other faiths
Pasta story; potatoes, maize, tomatoes, chillies from the Americas after 1492; Irish famine
Smallpox, silver, El Dorado, plantations and slavery, European migration
China retreats, Americas rise; Europe the centre of world trade

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: why people travelled, ancient links, the silk routes, food exchanges, conquest of the Americas, and the westward shift of world trade

slides.narration: Let us sum up. People have always travelled, for trade, work, faith or safety, carrying goods, ideas and germs. The silk routes linked Asia, Europe and Africa for well over a thousand years. Foods like potatoes and chillies crossed the oceans after fourteen ninety-two. In the Americas, smallpox did more than swords, silver enriched Europe, and enslaved Africans worked the plantations. Slowly, Europe became the centre of world trade.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Board scope: only the pre-modern world and conquest, disease and trade. The nineteenth century onwards is for the project.
Say "silk **routes**", plural: land and sea, many branches.
Precious metals flowed **from Europe to Asia** on the silk routes; American silver came only after the 1500s.
Smallpox: explain **why** (no immunity after isolation), not just that it killed.
Potato: give both sides, better diets and the Irish famine.
For contested stories (pasta), write "it is believed" or "one view is".
slides.narration: Before your test, check these points. Only two topics of this chapter are in the board exam, so master them. Always say routes, not route. Remember which way the gold and silver flowed on the silk routes: east, into Asia. When you write about smallpox, explain the lack of immunity. For the potato, give the benefit and the famine. And for uncertain stories like pasta, use careful words.

decks.title: The Making of a Global World — Part 2: 1815 to the 1950s (interdisciplinary project only)
goals: Trace global flows of trade, labour and capital from 1815 to the Bretton Woods era
Describe indentured migration from India and the role of Indian traders and bankers abroad
Explain the Great Depression and its effects on India
Plan a project display on one of these themes

slides.heading: From 1815 to Bretton Woods (project topic)
slides.body_md: This part is assessed only through the **interdisciplinary project**, not in the board paper. Use it to plan and research your project.

nodes.label: 1815–1914: the nineteenth-century world economy
1914–1918: First World War
About 1929 to mid-1930s: Great Depression
July 1944: Bretton Woods conference
After 1945: decolonisation

visual.alt: Timeline of Part 2: the nineteenth-century world economy from 1815 to 1914, the First World War from 1914 to 1918, the Great Depression from about 1929 to the mid 1930s, the Bretton Woods conference in July 1944, and decolonisation after 1945
visual.caption: Project topic, not in the board exam

slides.narration: This short part is your project companion. The board exam does not test it, but your interdisciplinary project may. We will race through a century and a half: the busy world economy of the eighteen hundreds, two world wars, a great depression, and the plan for a new economic order made at Bretton Woods. Take notes on anything that sparks an idea for your project.

slides.heading: Three flows that tied the world together

rows: Wheat and meat to Britain; cloth to Asia
About 50 million Europeans to America and Australia in the 1800s
British investment in railways and plantations abroad

visual.alt: Table of three flows: trade in goods such as wheat, meat and cloth; labour, with about 50 million Europeans emigrating to America and Australia in the nineteenth century; and capital, such as British investment in railways and plantations abroad

slides.narration: Economists describe three kinds of flow. Trade is the movement of goods. Labour is the movement of people looking for work; in the eighteen hundreds about fifty million Europeans left for America and Australia. Capital is money invested far away, such as British money building railways. A good project can follow one flow and show how it changed lives in two different places.

slides.heading: Food, technology and empire

nodes.label: Britain abolishes the Corn Laws (1846)
Cheap food imported; British farmers cannot compete
Land cleared for farming in America, Australia, Russia
Railways, steamships, telegraph; refrigerated ships carry meat
Colonies drawn in as suppliers and markets

visual.alt: Flow: Britain abolished the Corn Laws in 1846, imported cheap food and its farmers could not compete; land was cleared in America, Australia and Russia; railways, steamships, the telegraph and refrigerated ships moved food; colonies became suppliers and markets

slides.narration: Britain's Corn Laws had kept out foreign grain. When they were abolished in eighteen forty-six, cheap food poured in and many British farmers could not compete. Far away, forests and grasslands were cleared to grow grain for Britain. New technology made this possible: railways, steamships, the telegraph, and later refrigerated ships that carried meat across the oceans. Colonies became both suppliers and markets.

slides.heading: Rinderpest in Africa
slides.body_md: In the late **1880s** the cattle disease **rinderpest** reached Africa with infected cattle brought from British Asia to feed Italian soldiers in Eritrea.

nodes.label: Rinderpest arrives in East Africa
Spreads across the continent by 1892
About 90 per cent of cattle die
Africans lose their livelihoods
Forced into wage work on plantations and mines

visual.alt: Flow: rinderpest arrived in East Africa, spread across the continent by 1892, killed about 90 per cent of cattle, destroyed livelihoods and forced Africans into wage work on plantations and mines

slides.narration: Here is a grim example of how disease and empire worked together. Rinderpest, a cattle plague, reached East Africa in the late eighteen eighties and swept across the continent. About nine in ten cattle died. For people whose wealth was their herds, this was ruin. Colonial governments and planters gained: with their cattle gone, many Africans had to work for wages on plantations and in mines.

slides.heading: Indentured labour from India

rows: Eastern Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, central India, dry districts of Tamil Nadu
Closer home: Ceylon, Malaya; also Assam tea gardens
New cultures: chutney music, the Hosay festival in Trinidad
Nationalists opposed the system; abolished in 1921

visual.alt: Table: indentured recruits came from eastern Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, central India and dry districts of Tamil Nadu; they went to Trinidad, Guyana, Surinam, Mauritius, Fiji, Ceylon, Malaya and Assam; they faced hard work and few rights, created new cultures such as chutney music and Hosay, and the system was abolished in 1921

slides.narration: In the eighteen hundreds, hundreds of thousands of Indians signed contracts, called indentures, to work on plantations overseas. Many came from eastern Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, central India and dry parts of Tamil Nadu, and went to the Caribbean, Mauritius, Fiji, Ceylon and Malaya. Recruiters often misled them, and conditions were harsh. Yet they built new cultures, like chutney music in Trinidad. The system was abolished in nineteen twenty-one.

slides.heading: Quick check: rinderpest
slides.body_md: Choose the correct option.
slides.narration: Think about who lost and who gained when the cattle died.

slides.heading: Indian traders and bankers abroad

rows: Sold local and imported goods to tourists

visual.alt: Table: Shikaripuri shroffs worked as bankers financing trade; Nattukottai Chettiars financed export agriculture in Southeast Asia; Hyderabadi Sindhi traders set up shops in busy ports worldwide

slides.narration: Not all Indians abroad were labourers. Some were bankers and traders. The Shikaripuri shroffs and the Nattukottai Chettiars lent money that financed farming for export in Asia. Hyderabadi Sindhi traders opened shops in busy ports around the world. A project could compare the life of an indentured worker with that of a Chettiar banker in the same region, using maps and timelines.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: planning a project display
slides.body_md: Project question: *How did indentured migration shape Trinidad and Fiji?*
bullets: Step 1 — Narrow the question to one or two places and a period (for example 1845–1921).
Step 2 — Gather three kinds of evidence: a timeline, a map of routes, and voices (imagined diary entries, clearly labelled).
Step 3 — Link to other subjects: geography (routes and climate), economics (wages and sugar prices), language (chutney music).
Step 4 — End with a judgement: what was gained, what was lost.

rows: Key dates of recruitment and abolition
Routes from India to the Caribbean and Fiji

visual.alt: Table of a four-panel project plan: timeline, map of routes, imagined labelled voices, and a final judgement on gains and losses

slides.narration: A strong project asks a clear, narrow question. Pick one or two places and a period. Then gather three kinds of evidence: a timeline, a map, and voices. If you write imagined diary entries, label them clearly as imagined. Connect to other subjects, such as geography and economics. Finally, give your own judgement. Examiners of projects reward clear questions and honest, balanced conclusions.

slides.heading: War, depression and India

nodes.label: 1914–18: First World War; USA becomes a creditor
About 1929: Great Depression begins
World prices and trade collapse
India: exports and imports nearly halve (1928–34); wheat prices fall about half
Peasants still owe the same revenue; debts and unrest grow

visual.alt: Flow: the First World War made the USA a creditor; the Great Depression began about 1929; prices and trade collapsed; India's exports and imports nearly halved between 1928 and 1934 and wheat prices fell by about half; peasants still owed the same revenue, so debts and unrest grew

slides.narration: The First World War left Europe in debt and made the United States a lender to the world. Then, around nineteen twenty-nine, came the Great Depression. Prices and trade collapsed. In India, exports and imports nearly halved between nineteen twenty-eight and nineteen thirty-four, and wheat prices fell by about half. Yet peasants still had to pay the same revenue. You met the political result in the last chapter: civil disobedience.

slides.heading: Quick check: twentieth-century order
slides.body_md: Arrange these events from earliest to latest.
slides.narration: Put a year next to each event before ordering them.

slides.heading: Bretton Woods and after
slides.body_md: In **July 1944**, at **Bretton Woods** in New Hampshire, USA, the Allied countries planned a post-war economic order.

rows: Help countries manage shortfalls and surpluses in their foreign payments
International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (World Bank)
Fixed exchange rates; the dollar linked to gold at USD 35 an ounce
Later: newly independent countries form the Group of 77

visual.alt: Table of Bretton Woods decisions: the IMF to help countries manage their foreign payments, the World Bank for reconstruction, fixed exchange rates with the dollar linked to gold at 35 US dollars an ounce, and later the Group of 77 of newly independent countries demanding a fairer order

slides.narration: Towards the end of the Second World War, delegates met at Bretton Woods in the United States. They created two institutions, often called the Bretton Woods twins: the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. Currencies were tied to the US dollar, and the dollar to gold. Later, many newly independent countries felt the system favoured rich nations, and formed the Group of Seventy-Seven to press for change.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: turning facts into a project chart
slides.body_md: Task: *Show the effect of the Depression on an Indian peasant family, using imagined but realistic figures.*
bullets: Step 1 — Label the data as imagined.
Step 2 — Keep it consistent: if wheat prices fall by half, the same harvest earns half as much.
Step 3 — Show the squeeze: income falls, revenue stays the same.
Step 4 — Draw a conclusion and link to the Civil Disobedience Movement.

visual.alt: Imagined table for a peasant family: the same 20 quintals of wheat earned an income index of 100 in 1928 and 50 in 1932, while revenue due stayed at 20, so revenue rose from 20 per cent to 40 per cent of income

slides.narration: Data makes a project come alive, but it must be honest. If you invent figures, say so, and keep them consistent. Here the family sells the same wheat, but the price halves, so its income halves. The revenue does not change. So revenue rises from a fifth of income to two-fifths. That squeeze explains why so many peasants joined the Civil Disobedience Movement.

slides.heading: Quick check: Bretton Woods
slides.body_md: Choose the correct option.
slides.narration: Two institutions were born at this conference. Which option names them?

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2 (project topic)

rows: Corn Laws abolished; new technology; colonies as suppliers; rinderpest in Africa
Indentured workers to the Caribbean, Mauritius, Fiji; shroffs and Chettiars
War, the USA as creditor, the Great Depression and its effects on India
Bretton Woods: IMF and World Bank; G-77 demands a fairer order

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: three flows; the nineteenth century; Indians abroad; war and depression; and Bretton Woods and after

slides.narration: To sum up Part 2: trade, labour and capital tied the world together in the eighteen hundreds, helped by railways, steamships and empire. Indians went abroad as indentured workers, traders and bankers. War and the Great Depression shook the world economy and hit Indian peasants hard. At Bretton Woods, the victors built a new order, which newly independent countries later sought to make fairer.

slides.heading: Project tips
bullets: This part is **not** in the board paper; do not spend board revision time memorising it.
Choose a narrow question with a place and a period.
Label imagined data and voices clearly; keep figures consistent.
Link at least two subjects (history, geography, economics, language).
End with your own balanced judgement.
slides.narration: A last word on priorities. For the board exam, Part 1 matters. Part 2 is for your project. When you plan the project, choose a sharp question, use maps and timelines, label anything you imagine, and connect subjects. Finish with your own judgement, weighing gains against losses. That is exactly the kind of thinking the project is meant to reward.

notes.title: The Making of a Global World — Notes

sections.heading: 1. A world linked long before modern times
sections.body_md:
**Board scope:** only the pre-modern world (this section and the next) and conquest, disease and trade (sections 3–4) are examined. Section 5 is for the interdisciplinary project.

The world has been tied together for thousands of years by people on the move: **traders** seeking profit, **workers** seeking a living, **priests and pilgrims** travelling for faith, scholars seeking knowledge, and people **escaping persecution**. They carried goods, money, skills, ideas and inventions, and also **germs**.

**Early evidence**
- About **3000 BCE**: a **coastal trade** linked the **Indus valley** with present-day **West Asia**.
- **Cowries** (Indian Ocean seashells used as money) from the **Maldives** reached **China and East Africa**.
- Disease-carrying germs travelled long distances by at least the **seventh century**; by the **thirteenth century** the link with trade routes is clear.

**The silk routes**
- Not one road but **several routes over land and by sea**, joining Asia with **Europe and northern Africa**; in use from **before the Christian Era** almost until the **fifteenth century**.
- Named after **Chinese silk** carried west; Chinese **pottery**, and **textiles and spices** from India and Southeast Asia, went the same way. **Gold and silver** flowed from Europe **to Asia** in return.
- Trade and culture moved together: **Buddhism** spread from eastern India through the routes' meeting points; early **Christian missionaries** and, later, **Muslim preachers** travelled them.

sections.heading: 2. Food travels
sections.body_md:
Food shows how cultures borrow from each other across great distances.
- **Pasta:** one story holds that Chinese noodles were carried west and turned into Italian **spaghetti**; or that **Arab traders** took pasta to **Sicily** in the fifth century. The exact route is uncertain.
- **Foods from the Americas:** **potatoes, maize, tomatoes, chillies, groundnuts, soya and sweet potatoes** were first grown by the original peoples of the Americas. Europe and Asia first met them only about **five hundred years ago**, reaching them only after **Columbus** crossed the Atlantic in **1492**. Chillies are believed to have reached India with **Portuguese** traders in the sixteenth century.
- **The potato** gave Europe's poor a cheap, filling food: many were **better fed and lived longer**. But Ireland's poorest peasants came to depend on it almost entirely. When **blight** destroyed the crop in the **mid-1840s**, **hundreds of thousands starved** and many emigrated.

key_terms.definition_md: A plant disease that rots crops; it destroyed Ireland's potatoes in the 1840s.
The main food that a people depend on every day.

sections.heading: 3. Conquest, disease and trade in the sixteenth century
sections.body_md:
- In the sixteenth century European sailors found a **sea route to Asia** and crossed the **Atlantic** to the **Americas**.
- Before this, the **Indian subcontinent** was a **central meeting point** of Indian Ocean trade. European entry **expanded** some flows and **redirected** others **towards Europe**.
- The Americas had been **cut off** from the rest of the world for thousands of years. Their **precious metals, especially silver**, enlarged Europe's wealth and **paid for its trade with Asia**. Legends of **El Dorado**, a city of gold in South America, sent expedition after expedition looking for it.
- Spanish and Portuguese **conquest** of the Americas was well under way by the **mid-sixteenth century**. It did not rest on firepower alone: the most decisive force was **germs**, above all **smallpox**. With **no immunity** after their long isolation, local peoples died in huge numbers; the disease often spread **ahead of the Europeans** and devastated communities. Guns could be captured and turned against invaders; disease could not.

key_terms.definition_md: The body's ability to resist a disease, built up when a population has long lived with it.
A legendary city of gold in South America that many European expeditions searched for.
Taking control of a land and its people by force.

sections.heading: 4. Migration, plantations and the westward shift of trade
sections.body_md:
- Until the nineteenth century, **poverty and hunger** were common in Europe, cities were **crowded** and **deadly diseases** widespread, and **religious dissenters** were persecuted. Thousands left for **America**.
- **Enslaved Africans**, seized and shipped across the Atlantic, were forced to grow **cotton and sugar** on American plantations for buyers in Europe.
- Until well into the **eighteenth century**, **China and India** were among the **richest** countries and led Asian trade. From the fifteenth century **China**, by most accounts, **turned away from overseas contact**.
- China's reduced role and the rising importance of the **Americas** gradually moved the **centre of world trade westwards**; **Europe** became its centre.

key_terms.definition_md: A large farm growing one crop for sale, often worked by forced or bound labour.
A person who refuses to accept the official or majority religion.

sections.heading: 5. 1815 to the 1950s (interdisciplinary project only)
sections.body_md:
*Not assessed in the board exam.*
- **Three flows:** trade (goods), labour (people) and capital (investment). About **50 million** people left Europe for America and Australia in the nineteenth century.
- Britain abolished the **Corn Laws** (1846); cheap food imports followed and land was cleared abroad to grow grain for Britain. **Railways, steamships, the telegraph** and **refrigerated ships** carried goods.
- **Rinderpest** reached Africa in the late 1880s and killed about **90 per cent** of cattle, pushing Africans into wage work.
- **Indentured labour:** workers from eastern UP, Bihar, central India and dry districts of Tamil Nadu went to **Trinidad, Guyana, Surinam, Mauritius, Fiji, Ceylon and Malaya**; abolished in **1921**. Indian bankers and traders abroad: **Shikaripuri shroffs**, **Nattukottai Chettiars**, Hyderabadi Sindhi traders.
- **Great Depression** (about 1929 to mid-1930s): India's exports and imports nearly halved between 1928 and 1934; wheat prices fell by about half, while revenue demands stayed the same.
- **Bretton Woods (July 1944):** the **IMF** and the **World Bank**; fixed exchange rates with the dollar linked to gold. Newly independent countries later formed the **Group of 77**.

key_terms.definition_md: A worker bound by contract to work for an employer for a fixed period, usually far from home.
The IMF and the World Bank, set up at the 1944 conference.

**Board scope**
- Only the pre-modern world and conquest, disease and trade are examined. The nineteenth century onwards is for the interdisciplinary project.

**Common mistakes**
- Writing "the silk route" as one road: there were **several land and sea routes**.
- Getting the flow of precious metals backwards: on the silk routes **gold and silver went from Europe to Asia**.
- Saying potatoes or chillies were in India before 1500: they came from the **Americas** after **1492**.
- Stating that guns alone conquered the Americas: explain **smallpox** and the **lack of immunity**.
- Treating the pasta story as certain: write "it is believed".

**How marks are earned**
- Source-based (4 marks): (a) and (b) one precise fact each; (c) one point from the source and one from your knowledge, about 40 words.
- 3-mark answers: three distinct points, 40–60 words. 5-mark answers: five numbered points, about 120 words; for "evaluate", take a position and weigh a counter-point.

questions.stem_md: Long before modern times, people travelled great distances across the world. Which group of reasons best explains why?

options.text_md: Only to conquer new lands for their kings
Trade and work, learning, religious faith and pilgrimage, and escape from persecution
Only to collect taxes from distant regions
Only to escape from famines

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Traders, workers, scholars, priests and pilgrims all travelled: some for profit or jobs, some for knowledge, some for spiritual reasons, and some to escape persecution at home.
Step 2: So (b) is the complete answer.
Step 3: (a), (c) and (d) each name a single reason (conquest, taxes, famine) and use "only", which makes them false.

questions.stem_md: Evidence of an active coastal trade linking the Indus valley civilisation with present-day West Asia dates back to about

options.text_md: 3000 BCE
500 CE

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Coastal trade between the Indus valley and West Asia goes back to about **3000 BCE**, so (a).
Step 2: 1492 is the year Columbus reached the Americas; the other dates are far too late for the Indus civilisation.

questions.stem_md: Cowries were used as a form of currency in the pre-modern world. Where did they come from, and where did they travel?

options.text_md: Gold coins from Spain that reached Mexico
Silver coins from China that reached Europe
Seashells from the Maldives that reached China and East Africa
Copper coins from Rome that reached India

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Cowries are **seashells** from the Indian Ocean. Shells from the **Maldives** were carried as far as **China and East Africa**, where they served as money.
Step 2: So (c). The other options describe metal coins, not cowries.

questions.stem_md: Why do historians call the ancient trade networks across Asia the "silk routes"?

options.text_md: Because silk was the only good carried on them
Because the roads were paved with silk
Because they were built by the Roman emperors to import silk
Because Chinese silk carried westwards was one of the most valued cargoes on them

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The name highlights the importance of **silk from China** carried west along these routes, so (d).
Step 2: (a) is wrong: pottery, spices, textiles, precious metals and ideas also moved along them. (b) is absurd, and (c) is false: the routes were many and grew up over centuries through traders of many lands.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following correctly shows a flow of goods along the pre-modern silk routes?

options.text_md: Gold and silver from Europe to Asia
Potatoes from China to Ireland
Silver from America to China in 500 CE
Tomatoes from India to Mexico

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Silk, pottery, textiles and spices travelled west from Asia; in return **precious metals, gold and silver, flowed from Europe to Asia**. So (a).
Step 2: Potatoes and tomatoes came from the Americas and reached the rest of the world only after 1492; American silver reached Asia only after the sixteenth century.

questions.stem_md: For roughly how long did the silk routes flourish?

options.text_md: Only during the nineteenth century
From before the Christian Era almost until the fifteenth century
From 1492 to 1914
Only after the Portuguese reached India

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The silk routes were in use **before the Christian Era** and remained important **almost till the fifteenth century**, so (b).
Step 2: The other options are periods of later, European-led trade.

questions.stem_md: A traveller in the year 650 CE meets a Buddhist monk at an oasis town on a caravan route between China and Central Asia. What does this meeting best show about the silk routes?

options.text_md: They were used only by soldiers.
They had been replaced by sea routes to America.
They were closed to people from India.
They carried ideas and religions along with goods.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: **Buddhism** travelled out of eastern India along these routes to Central Asia, China and beyond.
Step 2: Trade and culture moved together, so (d).
Step 3: Christian missionaries and, a few centuries later, Muslim preachers also travelled these routes. The other options are false.

questions.stem_md: The popular story that noodles travelled west from China and became spaghetti in Italy is an example of

options.text_md: how foods carried by traders and travellers changed cooking in distant lands
how European conquest spread diseases
how the Corn Laws changed British farming
how the silk routes declined after the fifteenth century

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Whether noodles went west from China, or Arab traders took pasta to Sicily, the story shows foods moving with travellers and being changed to suit local taste.
Step 2: That is long-distance cultural exchange through food, so (a). The other options are unrelated.

questions.stem_md: Which of these foods was **unknown** in India until after Europeans reached the Americas?

options.text_md: Rice
Wheat
Chilli
Lentils

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Chillies, along with potatoes, tomatoes, maize, groundnuts, soya and sweet potatoes, reached Asia and Europe only after Columbus reached the Americas in 1492.
Step 2: Chillies are believed to have been brought to India by Portuguese traders in the sixteenth century. So (c).
Step 3: Rice, wheat and lentils had been grown in India for thousands of years.

questions.stem_md: Which group consists **only** of foods that came from the Americas?

options.text_md: Potato, maize, groundnut, tomato
Potato, rice, groundnut, tea
Maize, wheat, tomato, mango
Chilli, sugarcane, banana, potato

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Potatoes, maize, groundnuts and tomatoes were all first grown by the peoples of the Americas.
Step 2: Rice, tea, wheat, mango, sugarcane and banana originated in Asia or nearby regions. So (a).

questions.stem_md: Why did hundreds of thousands of people in Ireland die of starvation in the mid-1840s?

options.text_md: The Corn Laws banned the import of potatoes.
Smallpox brought by Spanish sailors spread through Ireland.
The poorest peasants depended so heavily on potatoes that a disease destroying the crop left them with almost nothing to eat.
Ireland stopped trading with America.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The potato had become the staple food of Ireland's poorest peasants. When a plant disease (blight) destroyed the crop in the mid-1840s, they had little else to eat.
Step 2: So (c). This shows the danger of depending on a single crop.
Step 3: (a) and (d) are invented; (b) confuses the famine with the conquest of the Americas.

questions.stem_md: An imagined village record from northern Europe in the late eighteenth century notes that families now eat better and fewer children die young. Which change is most likely to explain this?

options.text_md: The arrival of the potato, a cheap and filling crop from the Americas
The opening of the Suez Canal
The invention of the telegraph
The end of the silk routes

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The potato, brought from the Americas, gave Europe's poor a cheap, nourishing food; many were better fed and lived longer.
Step 2: So (a).
Step 3: The Suez Canal (1869) and the telegraph are later and do not explain better diets in the eighteenth century; the end of the silk routes would not improve food supply.

questions.stem_md: Before the sixteenth century, what was the position of the Indian subcontinent in the trade of the Indian Ocean?

options.text_md: It was cut off from ocean trade.
It traded only with Europe.
It traded only through the Portuguese.
It was a central meeting point in the busy trade networks of the region.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Goods, people and ideas from many lands met in Indian ports; the subcontinent was central to the flows of trade around the Indian Ocean.
Step 2: So (d).
Step 3: When Europeans arrived in the sixteenth century, they enlarged parts of this trade and steered other parts towards their own ports.

questions.stem_md: How did the precious metals of the Americas, especially silver, affect Europe?

options.text_md: They were used only to build churches in America.
They had no effect, because they stayed in the mines.
They were sent to Africa to buy cattle.
They made Europe richer and paid for its trade with Asia.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Silver mined in the Americas (for example in present-day Peru and Mexico) flowed to Europe.
Step 2: It increased Europe's wealth and paid for its purchases of Asian goods, so (d).

questions.stem_md: El Dorado was

options.text_md: a Portuguese trading port in India
the first ship to cross the Atlantic
a legendary city of gold in South America that many European expeditions searched for
a Spanish law about silver mines

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Stories of **El Dorado**, a city of gold somewhere in South America, drew many European expeditions.
Step 2: The legend shows how the hope of precious metals drove conquest. So (c).

questions.stem_md: Which was the most decisive "weapon" of the Spanish and Portuguese in conquering the Americas in the sixteenth century?

options.text_md: Cannons mounted on ships
Horses and armour
Germs of diseases such as smallpox, to which the local people had no immunity
Treaties signed with local rulers

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: After thousands of years of isolation, the peoples of the Americas had no immunity to diseases common in Europe.
Step 2: **Smallpox** spread ahead of the conquerors and wiped out whole communities, so (c).
Step 3: Guns and horses mattered, but weapons could be captured and turned against the invaders; disease could not be fought that way.

questions.stem_md: Smallpox killed far more people in the Americas than in Europe. What is the best explanation?

options.text_md: Smallpox was a disease that affected only Americans.
The Americas had been isolated from Europe, Asia and Africa for a very long time, so their peoples had no immunity.
Europeans had invented a cure for smallpox in the sixteenth century.
The Americas had a colder climate.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Immunity builds up in populations that have long lived with a disease. Europeans had; the peoples of the Americas, cut off for millennia, had not.
Step 2: So (b).
Step 3: (a) is false; (c) is false (vaccination came only in the late eighteenth century); (d) is irrelevant and untrue for most of the region.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following did **not** push people to leave Europe for America before the nineteenth century?

options.text_md: Poverty and hunger
Crowded cities and widespread deadly diseases
Persecution of religious dissenters
The promise of free land in Asia offered by China

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Until the nineteenth century, poverty, hunger, crowded and disease-ridden cities, and religious persecution drove thousands from Europe to America.
Step 2: China made no such offer; in fact China was limiting its overseas contacts. So (d).

questions.stem_md: By the eighteenth century, plantations in the Americas growing cotton and sugar for European markets were worked mainly by

options.text_md: enslaved people captured in Africa
indentured labourers from India
Chinese merchants
European soldiers

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Africans were seized, **enslaved** and shipped across the Atlantic to work these plantations, so (a).
Step 2: Indian indentured labourers went to the Caribbean mainly after slavery was abolished, in the nineteenth century.

questions.stem_md: Until well into the eighteenth century, which countries were among the richest in the world and leading powers in Asian trade?

options.text_md: Britain and France
Spain and Portugal
China and India
Ireland and Italy

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Right up to the 1700s, **China and India** ranked with the wealthiest lands on earth and dominated Asian trade.
Step 2: So (c).

questions.stem_md:
Consider two statements.

**I.** From the fifteenth century China, by most accounts, began to turn away from overseas contact.

**II.** The Americas grew in importance as a source of silver, crops and markets.

Together, what did these two developments lead to?

options.text_md: The rise of the silk routes
The shift of the centre of world trade westwards, towards Europe
The end of European trade with Asia
The isolation of the Americas

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: China's reduced role and the rising importance of the Americas gradually moved the centre of world trade westward.
Step 2: Europe emerged as its centre, so (b).

questions.stem_md: An imagined ship's log, dated October 1492, records sailors sighting land after crossing the Atlantic westward from Spain. Which change in world history did this voyage begin?

options.text_md: The opening of the silk routes
The first trade between the Indus valley and West Asia
Regular contact between the Americas and the rest of the world, with exchanges of crops, people, metals and germs
The end of the Great Depression

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: In 1492 Christopher Columbus, sailing for Spain, reached islands of the Americas while trying to find a western route to Asia.
Step 2: This opened lasting contact between the Americas and Europe, Africa and Asia: foods, silver, settlers, enslaved people and diseases now crossed the ocean. So (c).

questions.stem_md: Which of these was **not** a feature of the pre-modern world before the sixteenth century?

options.text_md: Silk and pottery carried west from China
Cowries from the Maldives used as money far away
Buddhism spreading through the meeting points of trade routes
Potatoes feeding the poor of Europe

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Silk, cowries and the spread of Buddhism all belong to the pre-modern world of trade.
Step 2: Potatoes came from the Americas and reached Europe only after 1492; they became a staple of the poor much later. So (d).

questions.stem_md: Imagine a spice trader in Calicut around 1530 who notices that more and more pepper is now loaded on ships bound for Lisbon, instead of on ships bound for ports of the Red Sea. What is this trader seeing?

options.text_md: The beginning of the silk routes
The redirection of Indian Ocean trade towards Europe after Europeans found a sea route to Asia
The effects of the Great Depression
The Bretton Woods system

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: After Europeans, starting with the Portuguese, found a sea route to Asia, they entered the old Indian Ocean trade.
Step 2: Europeans enlarged parts of this trade and **steered** other parts towards their own ports, as the trader notices. So (b).
Step 3: The silk routes are far older; the Depression and Bretton Woods belong to the twentieth century.

questions.stem_md:
*(Interdisciplinary project topic: practice only, not assessed in the board exam.)*

In nineteenth-century Britain, the Corn Laws were abolished. What did these laws do?

options.text_md: They allowed the free import of corn from America.
They restricted the import of corn into Britain.
They forced Indian farmers to grow corn.
They fixed the price of silk in Europe.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The Corn Laws restricted corn imports, keeping food prices high in Britain.
Step 2: Industrialists and town dwellers pressed for their abolition (1846), after which cheaper food was imported. So (b).

questions.stem_md:
*(Interdisciplinary project topic: practice only, not assessed in the board exam.)*

Rinderpest, a cattle disease that reached Africa in the late 1880s, helped colonial powers because

options.text_md: it killed about 90 per cent of the cattle, destroying livelihoods and forcing Africans into wage work
it made African cattle immune to all diseases
it increased the price of African gold
it stopped Europeans from entering Africa

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Rinderpest killed roughly 90 per cent of Africa's cattle.
Step 2: With their main resource gone, Africans were pushed into working for wages on European plantations and mines, which suited colonial governments. So (a).

questions.stem_md:
*(Interdisciplinary project topic: practice only, not assessed in the board exam.)*

The Bretton Woods conference of July 1944 set up

options.text_md: the League of Nations and the Corn Laws
the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank
the East India Company
the Group of 77

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The conference at Bretton Woods, New Hampshire (USA), created the **IMF** and the **International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (World Bank)**.
Step 2: So (b). The Group of 77 was formed later by developing countries.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Smallpox often spread deep into the Americas ahead of the European conquerors themselves.

**Reason (R):** The original peoples of the Americas had no immunity to diseases brought from Europe.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true: the disease travelled from community to community faster than the invaders.
Step 2: R is true and explains A: with no immunity, every contact passed the infection on and whole communities fell ill. So (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Early Christian missionaries and later Muslim preachers travelled along the silk routes.

**Reason (R):** The silk routes linked Asia with Europe and northern Africa.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true.
Step 2: R is true, and it is why preachers used these routes: the routes connected the regions they wanted to reach. So (a).

**Assertion (A):** When blight destroyed the potato crop in the mid-1840s, hundreds of thousands of people in Ireland starved.

**Reason (R):** The potato had originally been grown by the peoples of the Americas.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.stem_md: Why did gold and silver flow from Europe to Asia along the pre-modern trade routes?

options.text_md: Asian rulers taxed every European traveller in gold.
Europe had no gold or silver of its own.
Gold was worth less in Europe than in Asia.
Europeans wanted more Asian goods such as silk and spices than Asians wanted European goods, so Europe paid the difference in precious metals.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Silk, pottery, textiles and spices were in great demand in Europe; Europe had fewer goods that Asian buyers wanted.
Step 2: To pay for what it bought, Europe sent gold and silver east. So (d).
Step 3: (a) and (c) are invented; (b) is false, Europe did have some precious metals, and later American silver added to them.

questions.stem_md: Which piece of evidence best supports the claim that germs travelled with traders **long before 1492**?

options.text_md: Historians can trace the long-distance spread of disease-carrying germs to at least the seventh century.
Smallpox swept through the Americas in the sixteenth century.
Rinderpest killed most of Africa's cattle in the 1890s.
Blight destroyed Ireland's potatoes in the 1840s.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The claim is about the period **before 1492**.
Step 2: Only (a) refers to that period; it dates the long-distance spread of germs to at least the seventh century.
Step 3: (b), (c) and (d) are all true events, but they happened after 1492, so they cannot support the claim.

questions.stem_md: An imagined farmer in Bihar around 1750 grows maize on one field and chillies on another. What made this possible?

Step 3: The silk routes linked Asia and Europe, not the Americas; the Corn Laws and cowries are unrelated.

(iii) Both caused **mass deaths** and led to **conquest** in the Americas and **emigration** from Ireland.
